posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
I will preface this by saying that if the game is good and I like it, then the more content the better. I like lots of things to do with lots of options for game play.
But I have also played games where the side quests just felt like a slog or a chore. And, as a player, I definitely suffer from FOMO (the fear of missing out). If there is something to do in the game, I feel the need to do it. My default mental perspective is why would it be in the game if it wasn't important to the game.
When it comes to how much to put into the game, I would ask myself things such as:
How involved are these missions/quests and how long do they take?
How many would you potentially have at one time?
How are they tracked so you can refer back to what you need to do, see directives, hints, etc.?
How can you keep track of what is completed and what is still incomplete?
Are they interesting quests or just very basic and time consuming?
How difficult are they and are they a pain in the ass to complete?
Do the quests require a lot of running back and forth and wasting time to complete them?
Are any of the quests timed or can you complete them without a time pressure?
Do any of the quests keep you from advancing?
Do they become tedious and distracting or are they still fun and exciting to uncover and complete?
Are they just there to pad the game or are they there because you think they will be engaging for the player and interesting to complete?
Do the quests go along with the story lines and makes sense or would the player get the feeling that they are just there to add stuff that really isn't necessary and they actually detract from the main story line?
Can they be skipped?
Are there any negative ramifications if a player chooses NOT to do some?
If some are mandatory and some are optional, can the player reasonably tell the difference?
Depending on the answer to these types of questions, as a player, I might say give me as many as you can. Or, I might have the opposite reaction.
Everyone is going to have their own unique perspective on this and a factor that turns off one player might be appreciated by another.
I plan on giving my players are much to do as I reasonably can as long as it still feels fun. And I think that is the key.
Would you, as a player, enjoy doing all these quests? Do they further the story and breath more life into the world that you created?
I think it would also be extremely helpful to get some input from play testers on this type of thing.
Anyway, not sure if that helps, but good luck on your project and remember to enjoy what you do!

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
For me, a story junkie, the point at which "you have too many sidequests" is the point when "your sidequests add nothing to the game except XP and Loot".
If you don't have anything interesting to say with a sidequest... I prefer it just not exist.
This is how I decide if I should make a sidequest or not.
Do I have an interesting story to tell?  No?  No quest then.
I do have some "mandatory" sidequests, but they each follow their own storyline and add to that narrative.  On top of which, they upgrade the skills of the characters, so there's at least a decent reward if the player doesn't find the stories compelling.
Anything else is just "Engage with the narrative".

posts.author: JohnDoeGames

A large game is amazing. Just make sure it isn't all the same, or all very different. It must feel like 1 universe, while all locations feel unique.
As long as you make a large enough story or enough side stories, bigger can be better. But then again, opinions are wide spread on topics like this. Some people just like short games and play 3 different games a week, others like to play one game for months.
No matter if you make a huge game, or a tiny game, there will always be players who'd wish you'd go the other way around.

posts.author: kirbwarrior
posts.body:
The most important answer is "More than the dev wants to make". You can see this in even high budget games where there are quests where the devs were either just going through the motions or were asleep at the wheel. If you have 17 amazing quest ideas, don't make 18. There's also the note I've heard in a lot of games of "make the game smaller than the player wants". You want the player to like the game and return to it, not to get bored of it.
...I had a much longer list of things to consider, but no. You're going to get bored of making your game at some point. You're going to get tired of playtesting the same quest over and over and over and over again. You'll know when you've hit the point of making something only for the sake of making it instead of having intention behind making it. You don't want to make the same mistake I see a lot of AAA developers make of having more map than game and more quest than story.
